aboutMe.baking: I learned to bake bread in 2020 and I've been baking ever since. I learned to scale recipes by hand but then I thought to myself, "Self. You're a web dev why don't you make a web app that does this for you?" So here it is.
aboutMe.expertise: My expertise is in JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. When it comes to JavaScript frameworks I've only used React but I would consider myself very knowledgeable about frontend code regardless of framework. The web did exist before the frameworks after all. I'm confident I can work in any JavaScript framework there is. I'm passionate about accessibility, I really enjoy building web pages that can be traversed with the keyboard because that is how I prefer to surf the web myself, no mouse necessary. I also enjoy thinking about how to make the user experience more enjoyable, intuitive and less frustrating. If you want to know specifics about my work history feel free to download my CV! Hope you enjoy the site. I've been maintaining it regularly now for a year. I have a roadmap to add several features that will make it easier to use and help me expand my knowledge and skillset.
aboutMe.site: First and foremost this website is a bread recipe scaler. Want to try a new bread recipe but don't want to make 20 rolls? Enter your recipe and then enter the amount of dough you need and voilà! The new measurements for the recipe get printed to new inputs. This will reliably scale up or down any bread recipe you have.
aboutMe.software: I also enjoy making software. Most of my experience has been on the web but I've done a little bit of everything. I started out as a C# dev in 2018, as an intern and my first real job was a Java shop but after that I noticed a trend in the company I was working at where the devs on my team were regularly not interested in doing the frontend work so I took it upon myself to own the frontend on that team and I've stayed on the frontend ever since.

getStarted.intro: Get started with baking bread can be <wave>easy</wave>. If you don't have any specialized equipment yet you can start with a simple recipe that doesn't require any special tools. And as you learn, you can decide if you want to invest in more tools.
getStarted.needs: Here are the ingredients you'll need for your first bake:
getStarted.next: Once you've mastered this recipe, you can start experimenting with different flours, adding seeds, nuts, other ingredients, and trying different baking techniques. If you are interested in learning more click next.
getStarted.scale: The most important thing to have is a kitchen scale. This will help you measure your ingredients accurately and consistently. You can find a kitchen scale at most stores that sell kitchen equipment. They are fairly inexpensive and will last you a long time.
getStarted.step1: Start by adding the water, yeast, and salt to a bowl and mix until the yeast is dissolved.
getStarted.step11: Remove the lid and bake for another 15 minutes.
getStarted.step12: Remove the bread from the oven and let it cool before slicing.
getStarted.step2: Add the flour and mix until the dough comes together.
getStarted.step3: Cover the bowl with a towel and let it rest for 12-18 min.
getStarted.step4: After the dough has rested, fold the dough over itself a few times.
getStarted.step5: Cover the bowl again and let it rise until the dough has doubled. This may take 1 to 2 hours.
getStarted.step6: Preheat your oven to 450 degrees Ferinheit or 232 Celcius.
getStarted.step7: Place your baking vessel in the oven to heat up.
getStarted.step8: Once the oven is preheated and the dough has risen, carefully remove the baking vessel from the oven.
getStarted.step9: Place the dough in the baking vessel and spray with water if you have a spray bottle and cover with the lid.
getStarted.units: This first recipe you'll learn I'll give you the ingredients in <wave>cups</wave> and <wave>tablespoons</wave> as well as grams. But as you get more comfortable with baking, you'll want to switch to using grams for more consistent results.
getStarted.vessel: You'll also need a baking vessel. You can use a dutch oven, a baking stone, or a baking sheet. If you don't have any of these, you can use a cast iron skillet with a lid or a large pot with a lid.

step1.formulaExplain: Generally flour is measured in grams and is the ingredient that all other ingredients are measured against. So the weight of the flour is always 100% and the other ingredients are expressed as a percentage of the flour weight.

step1.intro: This first lesson will cover bakers percentages. Bakers percentages are a way to express the ratio of ingredients in a recipe. Understanding bakers percentages will help you understand how to adjust a recipe to fit your needs. It also allows you to tweak a recipe you have to change the results you get to suit your tastes. It also allows you to create your own recipes.
step1.practice: To practice find a recipe you like and calculate the baker's percentages for each ingredient.
step2.benefits: Hydration helps bread last longer, have a better crumb, and a better crust. It also helps the dough be more extensible and easier to work with.
step2.examples: Some breads like focaccia and ciabatta have very high hydration levels. While other breads like bagels and pretzels have very low hydration. Pay attention to the hydration levels in the recipe and adjust as needed when you want to make your own recipes.
step2.flours: Not all flour can handle the same hydration levels. Whole wheat flour can handle more hydration than white flour and high protein flour can handle more hydration than low protein flour. Its important to use a high protein flour if you are making a high hydration dough.
step2.intro: The next lesson will cover dough hydration. Dough hydration is the ratio of liquid to flour in a recipe.
step2.liquids: This is easy to figure out if the recipe only contains water. If you add eggs, butter, oil, or other liquids you need to add those to the total liquid amount.
step3.alcohol: For those who don't drink alcohol, the alcohol is burned off during baking so there is no alcohol in the final product.
step3.bulk: Bulk fermentation is the first fermentation that happens after the dough is mixed. This is when the dough doubles in size. This can take 1 to 2 hours depending on the temperature of the dough.
step3.coldBulk: Cold bulk fermentation is when the dough is placed in the refrigerator to ferment. This can take 8 to 24 hours depending on the temperature of the refrigerator. This is used to develop more flavor in the bread. and it can really help you make bread fit into your schedule.
step3.final: The final fermentation is the fermentation that happens after the dough is shaped. This is when the dough rises to the final size before baking. This can take 1 to 2 hours depending on the temperature of the dough.
step3.flavor: The alcohol produced by the yeast gives the bread its flavor. The longer the fermentation the more alcohol is produced and the more flavor the bread has.
step3.longer: The longer the fermentation the more flavor the bread has. The shorter the fermentation the less flavor the bread has.
step3.rise: This is what makes bread rise. The yeast consumes the sugars in the flour and produces carbon dioxide gas. The gluten in the flour traps the gas and the dough rises.
step3.schedule: A very common pattern I use is to mix the dough in the evening and let it bulk ferment in the refrigerator overnight. I wake up follow my normal morning routine and go to work. When I get home from work I shape the dough and let it rise while I make dinner. Then I bake the bread after dinner to enjoy a nice homemade loaf during the week.
step3.scheduleWhy: This means I don't have to babysit a sourdough starter or spend all day making bread. I can make bread that is more flavorful than store bought bread and doesn't require a lot of time.
step3.sugar: The fermentation time is also affected by the amount of sugar in the dough. The more sugar the faster the fermentation. The less sugar the slower the fermentation.
step3.temperature: The fermentation time is affected by the temperature of the dough. The warmer the dough the faster the fermentation. The cooler the dough the slower the fermentation.
step3.what: The next lesson will cover fermentation. Fermentation is the process of yeast consuming sugars and producing carbon dioxide and alcohol.
step3.yeast: The fermentation time is also affected by the amount of yeast in the dough. The more yeast the faster the fermentation. The less yeast the slower the fermentation.
step4.autolyse: This process is called autolyse. Autolyse is a rest period that allows the flour to fully hydrate and the gluten to develop without kneading. This can take anywhere from 30 minutes to overnight. The longer the rest, the less kneading is required. Mix together the flour, salt and water in a bowl. Then let it rest covered at room temperature. The next day add the levain whether it be a sourdough starter or a poolish or instant dry yeast. Then mix the dough until the levain is fully incorporated. Then do the final fermentation and shaping. This method is great for beginners because it is less hands-on and requires less skill. But it does require more time and planning ahead.
step4.how: This section will go over how I knead dough by hand. There are many ways to knead dough, and you may find a different method that works better for you. So use that instead. But if you are new to kneading, this method is a good place to start.
step4.intro: This next lesson will go over kneading. Or if you are interested in no-knead techniques, skip to the bottom of the page and read the no-knead section.
step4.kneading: Kneading is the process of working the dough to develop the gluten. Gluten is a protein that gives the dough structure and elasticity. Kneading also helps to evenly distribute the yeast, salt, and other ingredients throughout the dough. without gluten, the dough would not be able to rise properly and would be dense and flat. Kneading is essential for most bread recipes if you plan to make the dough the same day. This task will be made easier if you have a stand mixer with a dough hook attachment. if you don't have a stand mixer, you can knead the dough by hand. To knead by hand, there is no right or wrong way to do it. The dough just needs to be worked until it is smooth and elastic. This can take 10-15 minutes. You can also use the windowpane test to check if the dough is ready. To do this, take a small piece of dough and stretch it between your fingers. If the dough stretches thin enough to see light through it without tearing, it is ready. If it tears, continue kneading. if you use a lower protein flour with a high hydration recipe the dough will be stickier and harder to work and will require more kneading. If you use a higher protein flour with a lower hydration recipe, the dough will be easier to work and will require less kneading. This problem can be exacerbated if you are using oil or butter in the recipe. The fat will coat the gluten strands and make it harder for them to develop. If you are having trouble kneading the dough, try letting it rest for 10-15 minutes and then continue kneading.
step4.noKnead: If you aren't interested in kneading, then you don't have to. But there is a trade-off. The dough will not be ready to bake the same day. Instead, you will have to let the dough rest for a long period of time. This can be achieved during cold bulk fermentation or a long room temperature rest if you are using a preferment and won't add the levain until the next day.
step4.slap.flour: Flour your work surface and hands.
step4.slap.lift: Lift the dough off your work surface so it folds over your hands
step4.slap.place: Place the dough on the floured surface.
step4.slap.scoop: Using both of your hands scoop under the dough so that your two middle fingers touch one another under the dough.
step4.slap.slap: Then slap the side closest to you onto the counter
step4.slap.turn: Then turning your hands 90 degrees relative to the dough repeat all steps
step4.trust: But trust the process, after 10 to 15 minutes the dough should be smoother and more stretchy than when you started.
step4.wet: This method is good for wet doughs because it requires less direct contact with the dough. If you are having trouble with the dough sticking to your hands, try wetting your hands with water instead of flouring them. This can help prevent the dough from sticking to your hands.
